ceramic.snippet:
In Sandoz Pharmaceuticals v. Richardson-Vicks, Sandoz sought a preliminary injunction against Richardson-Vicks, alleging that Vicks's advertisements for its Pediatric Formula 44 cough syrup were false and deceptive under the Lanham Act. Vicks advertised that Pediatric 44 began working instantly upon being swallowed, which Sandoz claimed was misleading because the active ingredient, demulcents, was not FDA-approved as effective for cough relief. Additionally, Sandoz contested Vicks's claim of superiority over competitors. The district court denied the preliminary injunction, finding that Sandoz failed to prove the falsity or deceptiveness of Vicks's claims and did not demonstrate irreparable harm. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit reviewed the case to determine whether the district court erred in these findings.

 The U.S.

 The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit reasoned that the Lanham Act requires a plaintiff to prove that advertising claims are either false or misleading rather than simply unsubstantiated. The court emphasized that the burden of proof lies with the plaintiff to demonstrate consumer deception, as the FTC is the entity with the authority to regulate and assess the adequacy of substantiation. The court noted that Sandoz failed to provide evidence of consumer surveys or expert testimony proving that Vicks's advertising misled the public. Additionally, the court found that labeling an ingredient as inactive does not automatically violate the Lanham Act unless the labeling is misleading, which Sandoz did not prove. The court deferred to the FDA's expertise on whether demulcents should be classified as active or inactive, noting that the FDA had not definitively classified them. Thus, the court affirmed the district court's decision, finding no clear error or abuse of discretion in its denial of the preliminary injunction.

Allergan moved for a preliminary injunction, which Sandoz argued was improper because the patents in suit were invalid and therefore there was no likelihood of success on the merits. Specifically, Sandoz asserted that the “wherein” clauses present in the independent claims of the patents in suit were not limiting because they “merely state[d] the intended results of administering Combigan[®] twice daily” and were not “material to patentability.

  Sandoz’s reference to case law for the proposition that “[a] whereby [or wherein] clause in a method claim is not given weight when it simply expresses the intended result of a process step” was unavailing. A Third Circuit panel has mostly reversed and remanded a district court ruling in a lawsuit brought by generic drug manufacturer Sandoz against proprietary drug manufacturer United Therapeutics Corp (UTC). The litigation concerned vasodilator drug treprostinil, which in the form relevant to the litigation, is continuously injected by a pump. When Sandoz sought FDA approval of its generic alternative to UTC's proprietary Remodulin®, UTC initiated patent infringement litigation against Sandoz. The patent litigation was settled, and Sandoz began a marketing campaign for its generic version; the marketing campaign ultimately failed after the UTC and the manufacturer of the cartridges restricted the sale of the cartridges to specialty pharmacies, to the exclusion of Sandoz. The district court also ruled in favor of UTC on Sandoz's claims that the UTC breached the patent litigation settlement agreement. On appeal, the Sherman Act and state consumer law rulings of the district court, along with a damages ruling, were reversed and remanded. The appellate panel affirmed the admission of Sandoz's expert's testimony, however ([_Sandoz, Inc. v. United Therapeutics Corp._](http://business.cch.com/ald/SandozIncvUnitedTherapeuticsCorporation1082026100826.pdf), No. 24-3067 (3d Cir. Oct. 7, 2026)).

**Background.** Vasodilator drug treprostinil, used to treat pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), can be administered orally, inhaled, or injected. Reports on patent litigation in the District of New Jersey — an ongoing series
By Paul W. Kalish and Jonathan J. Madara
![A courtroom with judge, lawyer, client and

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit has vacated a roughly $61.6 million judgment for Sandoz in its suit against United Therapeutics Corp. (UTC), holding that a patent settlement agreement's broad anti-interference language was too ambiguous for resolution on summary judgment when read alongside provisions excluding pumps and other delivery devices from Sandoz's license.

A New Jersey federal judge found on summary judgment that UTC’s conduct amounted to a breach and awarded damages, but the appellate panel ruled that the question of whether the settlement was breached must be decided at trial.

The District Court granted summary judgment to Sandoz as to liability on its breach of contract claim that UTC had violated the settlement agreement resolving the patent litigation with Sandoz and dismissed Sandoz’s antitrust and state tort claims. It awarded Sandoz about $61.6 million in damages after a bench trial.

The Third Circuit Court of Appeals reversed a $61.6 million breach-of-contract verdict against United Therapeutics Corporation (UTC) on October 7, 2026, and sent the underlying case back to the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey for further proceedings. The ruling, issued in Sandoz Inc. v.  
United Therapeutics Corporation (No. 24-3067), wipes out the prior damages judgment entirely rather than adjusting the dollar amount, meaning the question of whether UTC breached its settlement agreement with Sandoz will have to be litigated again, according to [MLex](https://www.mlex.com/mlex/antitrust/articles/2535158). This is not a consumer class action, and there is no settlement fund or claim form tied to it. It is a dispute between two drug companies over access to a drug-delivery device, and its outcome will determine how much, if anything, UTC ultimately owes Sandoz for delaying a generic version of the pulmonary hypertension drug Remodulin.
The appeals court did not simply recalculate the damages figure that a lower court had already trimmed once. Instead, it reversed the district court's grant of summary judgment on the breach-of-contract claim itself — the count that found UTC liable in the first place — and vacated the entire November 1, 2024 judgment, according to the [Third Circuit opinion text posted on CourtListener](https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/11013826/sandoz-inc-v-united-therapeutics-corporation/).

## Third Circuit Vacates $61.6 Million Patent Dispute Award, Affirms Antitrust Dismissal
Reports on patent litigation in the District of New Jersey — an ongoing series
By Paul W. Kalish and Jonathan J. Madara
![A courtroom with judge, lawyer, client and

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit has vacated a roughly $61.6 million judgment for Sandoz in its suit against United Therapeutics Corp. (UTC), holding that a patent settlement agreement's broad anti-interference language was too ambiguous for resolution on summary judgment when read alongside provisions excluding pumps and other delivery devices from Sandoz's license.
UTC had locked up the only cartridges that could deliver subcutaneous treprostinil (a treatment for pulmonary arterial hypertension), just as Sandoz prepared to launch its generic. A New Jersey federal judge found on summary judgment that UTC’s conduct amounted to a breach and awarded damages, but the appellate panel ruled that the question of whether the settlement was breached must be decided at trial.
The Third Circuit panel also held that UTC's supply-protection rationale defeated Sandoz's antitrust claims, even though UTC welcomed the harm to its rival. It revived a New Jersey tortious interference claim that does not depend on antitrust liability.

Because it did not have access to the cartridges, Sandoz launched an intravenous-only product in March 2019. Sandoz launched a subcutaneous version in May 2021 after the FDA approved an alternative cartridge. Litigation ensued. The District Court granted summary judgment to Sandoz as to liability on its breach of contract claim that UTC had violated the settlement agreement resolving the patent litigation with Sandoz and dismissed Sandoz’s antitrust and state tort claims. It awarded Sandoz about $61.6 million in damages after a bench trial.
